name: Saccardo's Slate
lede: Saccardo's Slate is a dark, blue-grey standard from Robert Ridgway's 1912 color book, most likely named for the Italian mycologist Pier Andrea Saccardo, whose own color chart was one of Ridgway's sources.

sections.title: A mycologist's color chart
sections.body:
Ridgway built his 1912 *Color Standards and Color Nomenclature* from about 4,000 named samples gathered from earlier systems [1]. Among them was Saccardo's *Chromotaxia*, a reference work by the Italian mycologist Pier Andrea Saccardo for naming fungus colors [1]. Saccardo's Slate and the related [[saccardo-s-violet|Saccardo's Violet]] most likely trace to that source, though no book we hold confirms this directly for either name [1][2].

Ridgway catalogued this slate on plate XLVIII, and the ISCC-NBS system of 1955 carries it as block 192 [2].

sections.title: The swatch
sections.body: Measured in LCH terms it is dark and low-saturation, lightness 36, chroma 11, hue 215 degrees [3]. Its nearest library neighbor is [[pale-charcoal|Pale charcoal]], about 2.8 units away, with the bluer [[dark-delft-blue|Dark Delft Blue]] close behind [3]. Next to [[slate]] it reads as the darker, bluer one [3].

sections.title: Field notes
sections.body: Our archive finds this slate, as photographed, in 295 of 23,781 paintings, about 1.2 percent, including Cezanne's 1899 *The Bathers* and a 1640 Indian miniature of Krishna diving into the river [4]. The earliest dated match is a 1270 Italian crucifix panel, a floor and not a first, since the archive's early centuries are thin [4]. These are computed color matches on aged, varnished paintings, not pigment identifications [4].

origin.named_after: most likely Pier Andrea Saccardo, Italian mycologist (1845-1920), author of Chromotaxia
origin.source: Ridgway, Color Standards and Color Nomenclature (1912)

questions.q: Saccardo's color chart, one of Ridgway's sources, was built to name the colors of what?
True or false: a book directly confirms Saccardo's Slate is named for Pier Andrea Saccardo.

openers: Saccardo's Slate likely traces to a chart built for naming the colors of fungi, not paintings.

issues: Naming tied to Saccardo's Chromotaxia by inference (Ridgway cites it as a source), not a direct book statement.
